environment: 12h; consensus anchor; no value process; three seeds per arm
mechanism_test: The law says income depends on the flow-to-dealer ratio rather than on either count. Holding that ratio at two while tripling both counts should therefore restore monopoly-level income. It does, on all three seeds: 224,792, 224,468 and 231,813 against the one-dealer figures of 229,615, 234,863 and 228,585.
ratio_law_errors: 1.1 to 3.2 percent at one dealer and two flow, and a consistent 5.4 to 5.7 percent under-capture at three dealers and six flow. The systematic gap at the larger configuration is unexplained and worth a look, but it does not affect the qualitative law.
verification_status: Three seeds per arm plus a mechanism test that could have broken it. This is the best-verified claim in the campaign.

why_needed: Every arm supporting FFA-67 used a fundamental anchor with a degraded index. 35 of the campaign's 68 stored configurations are unrunnable under the no-oracle law, including all boot_vol arms.
environment: 24h; consensus anchor; no value process; a passive ladder resting ten levels a side at 5 bps that never reprices; seeds 91 and 92
result: Confirmed and far starker than the oracle-era measurement. A ladder that never reprices earns between 4.3 and 5.0 million per member when the makers cancel before replacing, and loses money when they do not. The sign flips on both seeds.
reinterpretation: This is not really a property of the ladder. It is the cost of the quoting defect, measured from the other side. Cancel-then-replace hands roughly five million per member to any participant that simply stays in the book, because for part of every step it is the only depth there.
contrast_with_oracle_era: The earlier figures, plus 23.2 million against minus 5.6 million, mixed this effect with a configured volatility that no longer exists. The legal measurement isolates presence alone and is cleaner.

environment: 24h; consensus anchor; no value process; seeds 91 and 92 for the new arms, three seeds for the survival arm
design: The mechanism test was meant to measure how much of the ladder's income comes from being present: withdraw it halfway and expect roughly half the profit.
result: It did not measure that. Both withdrawal arms collapsed with the one-sided book failure, as did both arms of a control with no ladder at all. Cancel-first quoting cannot sustain a two-sided book on its own.

matrix.cancel-first makers plus a ladder for th: survives on three seeds; ladder earns 4,331,042, 4,957,434 and 5,334,756 per member
matrix.continuously quoting makers plus a ladde: survives on three seeds; ladder earns -83.62, -3,643.75 and 1,837.37 per member

reinterpretation: The ladder is not a parasite exploiting a gap in a functioning market. It is the only thing holding the market together under defective quoting, and its income is the price of that. The earlier framing, a presence monopoly extracting rent, had the causality backwards.
strengthened_claim: Cancel-then-replace quoting is not merely suboptimal, it is non-viable. A population of such makers has no two-sided book unless some participant stays resting continuously.

environment: 24h; consensus anchor; no value process; cancel-first makers with no continuously resting participant; two seeds at each maker count
result: Two, eight and sixteen makers per venue all collapse on both seeds, classified as COLLAPSED by the simulator's own two-sided-mark failure rather than inferred from a missing report. Eight times the makers does not meaningfully delay it.
contrast: Against three seeds surviving with a passive ladder present throughout, and three surviving with continuously quoting makers.
finding: Quantity does not substitute for continuity. What a market needs is not more liquidity providers but at least one that is present at every instant.
important_caveat: This may be a statement about synchronised quoting rather than about cancel-then-replace as such. Every maker in this runtime shares one quoting cadence, so they all vacate the book on the same phase. Real makers are not synchronised, and a population quoting on staggered cycles might cover each other's gaps. The finding as stated holds for synchronised populations; whether it survives desynchronisation is untested and needs per-maker quote intervals, which the configuration does not currently express.

environment: 24h; eight cancel-first makers per venue with nothing resting continuously; requote thresholds of 5 and 20 bps; seeds 91 and 92
measurement_of_the_caveat: With no threshold the makers requote about 3,511 times each per simulated hour and 97.6 percent of the steps that contain a cancellation have every maker cancelling at once. The population is synchronised despite holding different inventories, because the maker replaces its quotes whenever its target moves at all.
result: With a requote threshold all four arms survive, against six of six collapses without one. A 20 bps threshold cuts cancellations to 224 per maker per hour and drops the all-at-once figure from 97.6 to 7.1 percent.
finding: The collapse recorded in E-162 and E-163 is caused by synchronised quoting rather than by cancel-then-replace as such. The caveat attached to FFA-82 was the operative variable, not a hedge.
confound_not_yet_separated: The threshold changes two things together. Cancellations fall sixteenfold and synchronisation falls from 97.6 to 7.1 percent. Survival could come from fewer gaps or from other makers covering the gaps that remain. A one-maker arm separates them: with a single maker there is nobody to cover, so if frequency alone is sufficient it should survive, and if coverage matters it should still collapse while eight survive.

environment: 24h; cancel-first makers with nothing resting continuously; maker count against requote threshold; two seeds per cell
result: Collapse requires both more than one maker and synchronised requoting. A single maker requoting about 3,511 times an hour with no threshold survives, so high-frequency cancel-and-replace is not fatal by itself. Eight makers doing the same collapse. Eight makers with a threshold survive.
frequency_hypothesis_refuted: Reduced cancellation frequency is not the operative variable. The one-maker arm cancels at the full unthrottled rate and survives.
mechanism: Synchronised replacement makes makers trade against each other. When every maker cancels and resubmits on the same step, their new quotes cross their neighbours' not-yet-cancelled ones, which is the maker-versus-maker crossing measured at 19.8 percent of trades in E-132. That mutual crossing drains one side faster than the cycle restores it. A single maker has nobody to cross, and desynchronised makers meet a book that has already been rebuilt.
connects: E-132 measured the crossing and treated it as a volume artifact. It is also the collapse mechanism.

prediction: If the ladder's income was payment for covering gaps that lockstep quoting created, desynchronising the makers should erase it.
result: Confirmed. Ladder income falls from 4,331,042, 4,957,434 and 5,334,756 per member against synchronised makers to 7,543.68 and 12,249.10 against desynchronised ones, a reduction of about 99.8 percent.
conclusion: Continuous presence is worth almost nothing in a market whose makers do not vacate together. The entire presence premium recorded in E-161 was the cost of lockstep quoting, paid to whoever stayed in the book.

environment: 24h; seed 91; three venues; basic actors only: makers, noise takers and the arbitrage desks
what_worked: Spot is an emergent random walk with the three venues agreeing closely, and the triangular loop residual sits near zero apart from the excursions the desks trade.
defect_found: The dated futures basis diverges instead of converging. Two dated contracts each start at zero on listing and walk monotonically to about plus 4,000 bps against spot. The perpetual drifts to about minus 275 bps rather than oscillating near zero.
why_it_matters: A dated future is cash-settled against spot, so its basis must converge into expiry. The carry desks exist to enforce that and are not doing so. Self-anchored futures books price from their own trades, and nothing pulls them back.
honesty_note: The visualisation was requested to show arbitrage keeping spot and futures close. It shows the opposite, and is published saying so.

environment: 2h; seed 91; three venues; request budgets per participant class
round_one: Budgets set by guesswork bound on exactly one class. Triangular arbitrage was refused 1,422 times against a ten-second order budget while every other class saw zero refusals. Option dealers were unmetered because the tier list omitted them, and they were by far the heaviest requester at 461,518 admitted requests in two hours against 43,340 for the spot makers.
round_two: Budgets set from the measured rates, makers at 15 placements per ten seconds, collapsed the market. The primary book became durably one-sided and the run aborted.
round_three: Raising the maker budget to 25 collapsed it too.
mechanism: A requote is a cancel and two placements, so a maker replacing quotes every step needs roughly twenty placements per ten seconds per side pair. A budget below that does not slow the maker down, it stops it replacing one side of its quote, and the book empties. This is the same failure as FFA-83: what kills a book is not the rate of quoting but the inability to restore a side.
status: The window between binding and collapsing has not been found. Everything loose enough to leave the book alive is too loose to refuse anyone but the triangular desk.
note: Reported as a calibration failure rather than a null result, which is what the pre-registered falsifier required.

environment: 2h; seed 91; the placement budgets that collapsed the market in E-168, with a 20 bps requote threshold on the spot makers
result: Both budgets that collapsed an unthrottled market now survive, and the refusals land almost entirely on the takers.
maker_request_rates: Spot makers issue 222 requests in two hours at a budget of 25 per ten seconds, and 76 at a budget of 15, against 43,340 with no threshold. That is a reduction of two to three orders of magnitude, not the sixteenfold I estimated from the cancellation counts.
ffa87_falsified: Order-count budgets are not inherently incompatible with market making. The incompatibility was between budgets and unthrottled lockstep requoting, which is the same defect FFA-83 identified. A maker that requotes only when its target moves is the least affected class in the population.
ffa86_prediction_one_falsified: Requote-heavy makers were predicted to be hit hardest. With a threshold they are hit least, at zero refusals, while metaorder execution absorbs up to 78.9 percent.
ffa86_prediction_four_supported: A maker carrying a requote threshold was predicted to be affected far less, and is, by a wider margin than predicted.
economic_reading: A published order-count budget is a tax on takers rather than on makers, once makers quote sensibly. A maker expresses a standing intention with few messages and can absorb a budget by quoting less often. A taker's intent is the message: an execution algorithm slicing a parent order cannot batch its children, so metering placements meters its strategy directly. This is a mechanism worth stating carefully rather than a payoff figure, and it follows from message economics rather than from anything about edge.

environment: 2h; seed 91; a 15 placement per ten second budget; metaorder child interval varied from one second to ten
prediction_falsified: Coarsening the slicing was predicted to recover fills lost to the budget. It removes the refusals entirely, from 78.9 percent to zero, but recovers nothing: fills fall from 45.11 to 42.59 to 29.78 ABC.
why: There were no lost fills to recover. At one second slicing the trader was refused 79 percent of the time and still filled more than the version that was never refused, because its admitted request count was almost identical, 2,237 against 2,221. The budget capped attempts, not achieved trading, since the actor simply retried on the next tick.
correction_to_E169: The reading that budgets tax takers needs qualifying. Takers absorb the refusals, but a refusal is not a cost if the actor retries and the budget was not the binding constraint on its throughput. Refusal rate measures friction, not harm.
methodological: This is the second confound in the same measurement chain. Refusal counts were built to stop a payoff table confusing a class that declined to trade with one that was refused. They do that, but they cannot be read as harm either: a class refused four times out of five may trade as much as one never refused at all. Harm has to be measured in fills or payoff, with refusals only as the explanation.
caveat: One seed. The 45.11 against 42.59 gap is within what a single path can produce and no claim rests on its sign; the 29.78 at ten second slicing is a larger and more credible drop, and is explained by sending fewer children rather than by the budget.

environment: 2h; seeds 91 and 92; makers carry a requote threshold so the book survives; only the arbitrage desks are budgeted, at four placements per ten seconds
result: The carry desk is worse off under the budget on both seeds, by 51.7 and 30.1 percent, at refusal rates of only 4.5 and 12.5 percent. The metaorder trader was refused 78.9 percent in E-170 and lost nothing.
reading: Consistent with intent that expires. A carry desk refused at the instant a basis dislocation exists cannot retry into the same opportunity, so a small refusal rate lands on precisely the requests that carried the edge. A parent order still needs filling a second later, so refusing four of its five attempts costs attempts rather than trades.
strength_and_limits: Two seeds, one desk, and the same direction on both.
The carry desk loses money in every arm, so this measures a strategy becoming more unprofitable rather than a profitable one being taxed.
Triangular and dated carry desks traded nothing in this configuration, so the test rests on the spot-perpetual carry desk alone.
The intended refusal rate was about half; the achieved rate was 4.5 to 12.5 percent, which makes the effect per refused request larger than designed rather than smaller.
status: Supported directionally, not established. Needs a profitable desk, more seeds, and a refusal rate matched between the two classes before the contrast can carry weight.

environment: 2h; seeds 91, 92 and 93; makers carrying a 20 bps requote threshold; one class budgeted at a time
intended: Match refusal rates across an expiring-intent class (triangular arbitrage) and a retrying class (metaorder execution), then compare payoff change.
what_happened: The expiring arm produced no data. The triangular desks issued six requests each over two hours, against 4,940 in the configuration where they were profitable, so there was nothing to refuse and nothing to measure.
cause: The base configuration gives every maker a requote threshold. All three books then go stale together, the triangular loop stays internally consistent, and no dislocation appears. The requote threshold that rescues a market under a request budget also removes the arbitrage the triangular desk exists to trade.

retrying_half_confirmed.reading: Mixed signs across three seeds at a steady 18.4 percent refusal rate, which is what no effect looks like. This confirms the retrying half of FFA-89 on three seeds: an actor whose intent survives loses attempts rather than trades.

status: The discriminating comparison remains unrun. It needs a base configuration in which an expiring-intent class is active and profitable, which the requote threshold precludes.

motivation: Four consecutive experiments were undermined by a property of the base configuration rather than by their hypothesis: a class that never traded, a class left unmetered, budgets that collapsed the book, and a requote threshold that erased the arbitrage under study. Each was found one failed arm at a time, after the run.
tool: tools/characterize_run.py profiles a configuration before comparisons are run on it: requests issued, requests refused, and active result per class, flagging classes that never traded as uncomparable.
first_application: Profiling the configuration used for the last three experiments shows three classes that never traded at all, dated carry, futures makers and triangular arbitrage, and four more barely active: both cross-asset makers, the fixed-distance maker and the imbalance maker. Seven of sixteen classes could not have carried a measurement, and I had already attempted to measure two of them.
consequence: The matched-refusal design in E-172 was impossible in that configuration before it was run, and the profile would have said so in a few seconds rather than after nine runs.
rule_adopted: Profile a configuration and record which classes are comparable before designing a comparison on it.

goal: Build a configuration in which every participant class is active, so comparisons are not silently run on classes that never trade.
iterations: A four hour run left dated futures and futures makers with twelve requests each. The cause was the tenor: the short dated contract is listed on an eight hour cycle, so in a four hour run no dated contract exists at all. Shortening the tenors to two and six hours fixed it.
Removing the shared requote threshold restored triangular arbitrage from 18 requests to 59,028, confirming FFA-90: books that requote on one threshold go stale together and the loop stays consistent.
profile_of_the_reference: All seventeen classes active over eight hours. Triangular arbitrage 59,028 requests and plus 4,055 per member, futures makers 47,221 and plus 9,977, dated carry 2,516 and minus 7,857, option dealers 3,694,318 and plus 107,149.
tension_found: There may be no configuration that is both fully active and balanced. With a requote threshold the market survives request budgets but triangular arbitrage dies and makers barely trade. Without one every class is active but the makers are picked off catastrophically: carry arbitrage takes 112,455,084 per member from perpetual makers at minus 98,347,935 and spot makers at minus 74,585,526.
conservation: Population sum minus 2,427,692 against fee revenue 2,371,133 and no insurance payout, leaving a residual of minus 56,559, about 2.4 percent of fees and inside the band recorded in FFA-69.
tool_defect_found: The payoff table's member and per-member columns collided for values above a hundred million, printing 6112,455,083.94, which broke the profile's parser and would have silently dropped exactly the largest results from any automated reading. Widened.

environment: 8h; seed 91; four spot makers; requote thresholds shared, absent, or cycled across makers at 0, 10, 25 and 40 bps
result: Heterogeneous thresholds give the most triangular activity by a wide margin, 19,056 requests against 4,992 with no threshold and 1,824 with a shared one, and the only configuration where the desk makes money. Maker losses fall from 58.6 million per member to 1.4 million, forty times better than the unthrottled case though still far from the shared-threshold figure of plus 7,766.
mechanism_confirmed: Dislocation comes from books going stale at different times, not from books being stale. With no threshold every maker requotes every step and the books move together; with one shared threshold they freeze together. Only a mix leaves them drifting apart, which is what the arbitrage trades.
counterintuitive: The unthrottled configuration produces less triangular activity than the mixed one, which is the opposite of what more quoting would suggest. Synchronised movement is as consistent as synchronised staleness.
caveat: One seed, and the makers still lose 1.4 million per member under mixed thresholds, so this softens the tension rather than removing it.

environment: 8h; seeds 91, 92, 93; the reference configuration
result: All seventeen classes active. Six classes are sign-stable across three seeds and three of those are also magnitude-stable: option dealers within 0.8 percent, futures makers between 8,160 and 9,017, dated carry between -9,786 and -10,206.
cannot_measure: Triangular arbitrage returns 44, -135 and 14 per member across the seeds and noise flow returns -266,590, 80,785 and -592,876. Both change sign, so neither can carry a directional claim at this horizon, and both are classes earlier experiments in this campaign tried to measure.
carry_arb_precision: Sign-stable but spanning 2.7 to 19.8 million per member, so it supports whether it was harmed and not by how much.
published: research/reference-configuration-2026-08-17.md, to be cited with any comparison run on this configuration.

environment: 8h; seeds 91, 92, 93; the reference configuration; one class budgeted at a time
intended: Compare an expiring-intent class against a retrying one at matched refusal rates, using classes the reference profile says are measurable.
what_happened: The budgets bound on one seed each and not at all on the others. Where they bound, both classes improved: the dated carry desk by 15.3 percent at a 25.8 percent refusal rate, the metaorder trader by 8.2 percent at 3.6 percent.
why_improvement: Both classes lose money in every arm. Refusing a request from a negative-edge strategy prevents a losing trade, so throttling helps it. Harm cannot be measured on a class whose trading is unprofitable, because the budget and the strategy push the result in the same direction.
consequence_for_E171: The carry desk result in E-171, where a budget made a loss-making desk 30 to 52 percent worse, points the other way on the same kind of class. One of the two is noise, and the profile says carry arbitrage spans 2.7 to 19.8 million per member across seeds, so the earlier figures cannot separate a budget effect from seed variation.
structural_limit: The reference population contains no class that is profitable, magnitude-stable across seeds, and trading an intent that expires. Carry arbitrage is profitable and expiring but its magnitude is unstable; option dealers and futures makers are profitable and stable but express standing intentions; dated carry is stable but loses money. FFA-89 is not testable in this population as constructed.
status: Recorded as untestable here rather than reported as a null result.

how_found: A fills comparison returned numbers identical to the digit between the treatment and its control, which the research contract treats as a tooling failure until proven otherwise. It was.
defect: buildRequestPolicy chose a participant's tier by ranging over the tier map, so assignment depended on Go's randomised iteration order. A participant matching two tiers received a different budget on different runs.
why_it_hid: The reference configuration carries a deliberately generous all-roles tier purely to obtain request counts. Every narrower tier therefore overlaps it, and which one applied was decided at random on each run.
contaminates: E-177. Its budgets appeared to bind on one seed and not others, which was read as bursty request rates. It was the classifier picking the generous tier on some runs and the binding tier on others, so the refusal rates and the payoff changes drawn from them are not interpretable.
fix: Tier names are visited in sorted order and the longest matching role prefix wins, with a tier covering fewer roles preferred where prefixes tie, since that is the tier written to single a participant out.
note: The ratelimit package was audited for exactly this hazard and found clean. The defect was in the scenario wiring, which was not audited.

environment: 8h; seed 93; reference configuration; the dated carry desk capped at 300 placements for the run
result: A 35.3 percent refusal rate improves the desk's result by 26.2 percent, from minus 9,786 to minus 7,224 per member. The desk loses money, so preventing a third of its trades removes a third of its losses.
significance: This is a clean, deterministic measurement of the confound rather than of harm. Any payoff-based rate-limit claim about a loss-making class measures the sign of its edge, not the effect of the limit.
calibration_path: Four attempts were needed and each failed informatively. A ten-second order budget of one never binds on a desk that acts once every thirty-one seconds. A per-minute weight budget of one binds absolutely, because a subscription costs two and can never fit, so the desk never subscribes, never sees a book and issues twelve requests all run. A placement-only daily budget binds properly because subscriptions cost nothing against it.
practical_finding: A weight budget set below the cost of a subscription silently blinds a participant rather than throttling it. The participant is not slow, it is deaf, and its request count collapses to almost nothing, which looks like an inactive strategy rather than a misconfigured limit.

problem: Three experiments were run against a binary compiled before the fix under test. Each produced a result indistinguishable from a real null until something unrelated exposed it. The research contract warned about this after the second occurrence and the warning did not prevent the third.
fix: Every run records the version-control revision, build time and modified flag that Go embeds at build time. run_outcome.py compares the recorded revision against the current HEAD and reports STALE when they differ.
verified: A run from the previous commit is reported as STALE: built at af89e146, current source is 993fafcb. A run from the current commit is not.
second_order: Untracked build outputs made the modified flag true on every build, which masked the staleness message behind one that is true of almost every run. Build outputs are now ignored and staleness is checked first.
principle: A failure mode that survives being written into the contract needs a mechanical check, not a stronger warning.

environment: 8h; seed 93; reference configuration; placement budgets sized per class; fills counted from the event logs across spot and derivative books
result: For an expiring intent, refusals convert to lost fills almost one for one: 35.3 percent refused costs 35.9 percent of fills. For a retrying intent they convert to nothing, at 5.4 percent refused here and at 78.9 percent in E-170.
why_fills: Fills avoid the confound that made every payoff comparison in this line uninterpretable. A loss-making class improves when throttled, so payoff measures the sign of its edge; fills measure what the budget actually prevented.
limits: The refusal rates are not matched between the two classes, 35.3 against 5.4 percent. The comparison rests on the retrying class showing no fill loss at 78.9 percent in E-170, which is the stronger of its two measurements.
One desk represents expiring intent and one represents retrying intent; neither is a class of strategies.
tool_correction: fill_rates.py read only the spot book, so every fill table produced earlier in this campaign omitted option, perpetual and dated-future fills. With derivatives included the perpetual maker accounts for 24.8 percent of volume and the option dealer fills 14.0 percent of its 2.18 million orders, neither of which was previously visible.

environment: 8h; seeds 91, 92 and 93; reference configuration; dated carry capped at 300 placements for the run
result: Fill loss on all three seeds at comparable refusal rates. Direction consistent, magnitude between 0.55 and 1.09 times the refusal rate.
mechanism_test: The retrying class refused at 78.9 percent in E-170 lost no fills, which is the outcome that could have falsified the distinction and did not.

goal: Find or build a profitable expiring-intent class, since one desk currently stands for the whole category in FFA-89.
probe: Enabled the existing cross-venue routers, which are expiring-intent by construction: a dislocation between venues exists for an instant.
result_under_consensus: Zero executable signals in eight hours from either latency tier. The consensus index holds the three venues to within 0.004 of each other, so there is no dislocation to trade.
result_under_own_mid: 1,888 signals for the one-step tier and 1,151 for the two-step tier, every one submitted and completed, none failed. Payoff minus 13.31 per member.
latency_visible: The faster tier sees 64 percent more signals than the slower one, which is the latency race behaving as intended.
why_not_profitable: Both legs are crossed and pay taker fees, so a round trip costs about ten basis points. The dislocation the makers leave behind is smaller than that. A well-coupled market is precisely one where the remaining arbitrage does not cover its own costs.
expiring_intent_questioned: Every signal completed. If an opportunity always survives long enough to execute, the intent is not expiring in practice, so these routers are not the class FFA-89 needs even if they were profitable.
modelling_limit: Cross-venue latency cannot be shorter than one simulation step, so a latency race is resolved at one-second granularity. Sub-step races are not expressible.

environment: 8h; seeds 91, 92, 93; own_mid anchoring so venues are coupled only by participants; two router tiers at one and two steps of latency; 5 bps taker fee on each leg
result: The dislocation the routers capture is pinned at the round-trip transaction cost of ten basis points. The fast tier averages 10.40 and clears its costs on all three seeds; the slow tier averages 9.84 and does not on two of three.
interpretation: This is the no-arbitrage bound emerging from the population rather than being imposed. Arbitrageurs trade a dislocation until it equals what trading it costs, and stop. Nothing in the configuration sets ten basis points; it is the sum of two 5 bps taker fees, discovered by the participants.
latency_premium: One step of latency is worth 0.56 basis points, the difference between the tiers' average captured edge. That is also the difference between clearing costs and not, so the latency advantage is precisely what makes cross-venue arbitrage viable here rather than marginal.
answers: FFA-96's open question. The unprofitability of arbitrage in a coupled market is not a calibration failure but the equilibrium: a well-arbitraged market is one where the residual dislocation equals transaction costs by construction.

environment: 8h; seed 91; own_mid anchoring; cross-venue routers
design: Separate a cost-set bound from a competition-set one. Halving the taker fee halves the cost; doubling the routers doubles the competition. Only one of them should move the captured edge.
result: Halving the cost halves the captured edge, from 10.19 to 4.36 basis points, tracking the round-trip fee almost exactly. Doubling the number of arbitrageurs moves it from 10.19 to 9.42, a compression of 7.6 percent that leaves it at the cost floor.
conclusion: The bound is set by transaction cost, not by competition. More arbitrageurs compress the dislocation slightly toward the floor and cannot push it below, because below cost the trade does not pay and they stop.
secondary: Halving the fee nearly doubles the number of executable signals, since opportunities too small to clear a 10 bps cost clear a 4 bps one. Adding routers splits the same opportunities instead: the fast tier's signals fall from 1,888 to 1,176.
config_defect_fixed: The taker fee was hardcoded at five basis points in four places, which made the quantity that sets this bound impossible to vary. It is now a configuration field.

environment: 8h; seeds 91, 92, 93; own_mid anchoring; cross-venue routers
result: Across three seeds the captured edge tracks the round-trip transaction cost and is entirely unaffected by the number of arbitrageurs. Halving the cost takes the edge from 10.12 to 4.34 basis points. Doubling the arbitrageurs takes it from 10.12 to 10.13.
correction: The 7.6 percent compression attributed to competition in E-185 was single-seed noise. The four-router arm spans 9.42 to 11.09 across seeds, which brackets the baseline, and its mean is indistinguishable from it.
conclusion: Transaction cost sets the bound alone. Competition does not compress it even slightly, because an arbitrageur that would trade below cost does not trade at all.

environment: 8h; seeds 91, 92, 93 at each of three taker fees; own_mid anchoring; two router tiers
result: Captured edge equals round-trip transaction cost across a fivefold range, with a ratio between 1.01 and 1.09 over nine runs. The relation was tested downward first and then extrapolated upward, where it held.
why_slightly_above_one: The routers only fire when a dislocation clears their cost, so the edge they capture is the cost plus whatever the opportunity exceeded it by. A ratio a little above one is what that selection implies; a ratio below one would have contradicted the reading.
status: Nine runs across three cost levels and three seeds, with competition separately shown not to move it. This is the best-verified quantitative result in the campaign.

environment: 8h; seeds 91, 92, 93; reference configuration; a 5 bps taker fee, so a three-leg triangular loop costs 15 bps
result: A triangular desk firing below its own three-leg cost is worthless and sign-unstable. Raising the threshold above that cost makes it profitable on every seed and roughly seventy times larger in the mean, on half as many trades.
law_extended: The cost law governs the triangular loop as it governs the cross-venue one, with the cost being the sum of the legs crossed rather than a round trip of two. Three legs at 5 bps is 15 bps, and the threshold has to clear it.
corrects_the_reference: The reference profile recorded triangular arbitrage as unable to carry a claim because its result changed sign across seeds. That was not an inherent property of the class: it was configured to fire at 5 bps against a 15 bps cost, so it was trading loops that could not pay. With a correct threshold it is stable across seeds.
unblocks: FFA-89 needed a profitable, stable, expiring-intent class and the population appeared not to contain one. It did; the class was misconfigured.

environment: 8h; seeds 91, 92, 93; triangular desk with a threshold above its three-leg cost, so it is profitable and payoff is interpretable; capped at 1,100 placements for the run
first_finding: This is the campaign's first interpretable payoff measurement of rate-limit harm, because the class is profitable unthrottled. A budget refusing about ninety percent of its requests costs it twenty to thirty-three percent of its result on every seed.
second_finding: Payoff and fills move together, at minus 32.5 against minus 36.6, minus 25.3 against minus 20.1, and minus 19.8 against minus 20.6. That validates using fills as the proxy where payoff is uninterpretable, which is what E-181 had to do.
refinement: Harm is not proportional to refusal. Ninety percent refusals cost about a quarter of the fills, a ratio near 0.28, where the dated carry desk lost fills one for one at 35 percent refusals and metaorder execution lost nothing at 79 percent. The three classes sit on a spectrum rather than in two categories.
confound_not_resolved: The three budgets are not comparable. Each is an absolute cap for the run rather than a rate, and each binds at a different fraction of its class's demand, so the ratio may measure how the cap was set rather than how quickly each opportunity decays. Normalising the budgets is required before the spectrum can be read as a property of the strategies.

title: Refusal rate is not a valid dose variable: retry amplification makes it bimodal
design: Calibrate orders_per_day for triangle_arb, dated_carry_arb, metaorder_trader toward a common ~65% refusal rate on reference_base, 8h, seed 91.
finding: No cap yields ~65% refusal for triangle_arb. Between cap 1200 and 1300 the refusal rate jumps 96%->17% while total requests collapse 181236->8148 (22x). The desk retries refused orders, so refusals feed further requests: above the cliff the request stream is dominated by self-inflicted retries. Critically, admitted throughput is nearly flat across the cliff (7249 vs 6763), so two runs differing by 79 points of refusal rate deliver the same order flow.
implication: FFA-99 as designed is unanswerable. Normalising three classes to a common refusal rate cannot isolate strategy differences, because refusal rate measures each class's retry policy, not how much flow the exchange denied it. It also retroactively explains E-189's spectrum: triangle_arb's low fill-loss/refusal ratio (0.28) had an inflated denominator from a retry storm, not genuine denial. The 0-vs-0.28-vs-1.0 spectrum is not evidence about opportunity decay.
correction: Supersedes the dose variable used in E-181 and E-189. Harm must be regressed on admitted-throughput deficit (1 - admitted_budgeted/admitted_control), which is retry-invariant.
next: E-191 re-measures all three classes against admitted deficit.

title: Fill loss tracks admitted-throughput deficit one-for-one; the E-189 spectrum does not survive the corrected dose
design: reference_base 8h, log_mode full, seeds 91-92. Control (no budget) vs one budgeted arm per class: triangle_arb orders_per_day 1300, dated_carry_arb 200, metaorder_trader 4500. Dose = 1 - admitted_budgeted/admitted_control (retry-invariant, per E-190). Response = fill-count loss. Roles resolved from terminal_accounts client_id map; fills read from every venue log, not spot only.
finding: On the corrected dose, dated_carry_arb gives 1.02 and 1.03 across two seeds, and triangle_arb gives 1.08 at a 39% deficit. Denied a given fraction of admitted requests, both classes lose almost exactly that fraction of fills. Neither shows the retry-based recovery that E-189 attributed to triangular arbitrage.
caveats: triangle_arb seed 92 hit only a 4.8% deficit because the cap is an absolute number and demand varies by seed; its 1.71 ratio rests on a small denominator and should not be read as above-unity harm.

metaorder_trader is unresolved: 0.16 and 0.97 on two seeds is not seed noise around a value, it is disagreement about whether the class is harmed at all. Its earlier ~0 fill-loss ratio may have been a single-seed artifact.
Fill count, not payoff. E-189 showed the two track each other for triangle_arb only.
supersedes: The 0 / 0.28 / 1.0 fill-loss spectrum reported in E-189. That ordering was computed against refusal rate, which E-190 showed is retry-inflated.
next: Seeds 93-95 for control, metaorder and triangle to resolve the metaorder disagreement.

title: Rate-limit harm is set by the marginal value of the denied requests, not their number
design: Mechanism analysis of the metaorder_trader seed disagreement in E-191, using the E-191 logs for seeds 91-92. Decomposed the response into fill count, filled quantity, parents started, parent completion rate, and the accepted-to-fill conversion rate.
finding: metaorder_trader harm does not appear as failed executions: parents still complete 94-99% of the time under budget. It appears as fewer parents started, because throttled execution takes longer and fewer parents fit the horizon. Parent-throughput loss (17.6%, 35.9%) tracks filled-quantity loss (19.1%, 36.7%) closely, so fill count is the wrong response variable for a splitting agent. The seed disagreement is explained by waste: the desk fires marketable children that mostly do not fill, and in seed 91 the budget pruned the non-filling ones first, doubling the accepted-to-fill conversion from 16.5% to 32.9% and holding fill-count loss to 7.1% against a 44.9% deficit. Seed 92 had little waste to prune (15.8% to 17.8%) and lost in proportion.
generalisation: Harm from a request budget is governed by the marginal value of the requests it denies, not by how many it denies. A class whose requests are homogeneous in value loses one-for-one (dated_carry_arb, 1.02 and 1.03 in E-191). A class whose requests vary in value gets a cushion equal to the waste available to prune, which is a property of the run rather than of the strategy.
implication: This dissolves the search for a per-class harm coefficient. The coefficient is not a strategy constant; it is a function of how much of that strategy's request stream was already unproductive. It also means a rate limit can act as an execution filter, improving efficiency per request while reducing throughput.
caveats: Two seeds. Seeds 93-95 running for control, metaorder and triangle.

Filled quantity and parent throughput, not payoff. A pruned request stream could still be worse in cost terms if the surviving children pay more slippage; vwap and signed_impact are logged per parent and not yet analysed.
The waste itself may be a defect in the metaorder agent (children priced through the touch with a slippage cap that leaves them unfilled) rather than a property of real execution algorithms.
next: Test the filter effect on cost, not only throughput: compare per-parent vwap slippage and signed_impact between control and budgeted arms.

title: Request budgets cost throughput, not execution quality
design: Per-parent cost analysis of the E-191 metaorder arms, seeds 91-92: signed slippage of vwap against the mid at parent start, signed impact of end mid against start mid, child count, realised participation, parent duration.
finding: Median slippage is identical to two decimals between control and budgeted arms on both seeds, and impact stays within a tenth of a basis point. Parent duration does not lengthen (it falls on seed 91) while parents started drop 17.6% and 35.9%. The budget does not make an execution worse, and does not stretch it; it delays the start of the next one. Harm is entirely throughput.
caveats: Slippage here is under one basis point, so the invariance is measured on small numbers.
Pre-dates the INVALID_QTY fix in commit 4981384, but the cost measure is per-filled-parent and the defect only produced rejected children.

title: The metaorder waste cushion was a defect artifact and does not replicate
design: Re-ran control and budgeted metaorder arms on seeds 91-93 after commit 4981384 retired parents whose residual falls below the venue minimum. Same configs as E-191.
finding: Removing the malformed children cut the desk's control request stream by 24.7%. The accepted-to-fill conversion no longer improves reliably under budget: on seed 91 it falls from 27.1% to 21.3%, the opposite of the doubling reported in E-192. The filter effect does not replicate.
retracts: E-192's claim that a rate limit prunes low-value requests first and that harm is governed by the waste available to prune. That cushion was largely 8302 guaranteed-invalid children per run, a defect in the agent rather than a property of throttling.
survives: E-192's finding that harm appears as fewer parents started rather than failed executions. Parent-throughput loss still tracks filled-quantity loss on all three seeds (20.6/20.6, 14.9/13.9, 25.8/23.7).
methodological_finding: Per-seed ratios cannot answer this question. The budget is an absolute cap, so the dose it delivers varies by seed (10.8% to 30.1% here), and a ratio taken against a 10.8% denominator amplifies noise. More seeds will not converge an estimator built this way.
next: E-195 sweeps the cap within one seed to fit a dose-response slope, and re-runs dated_carry_arb, whose E-191 result shares the stale control.

title: The round-trip desk was absent, not one-sided; funding it restores inventory mean reversion
design: A/B of commit f37b702 on def_control.json, seeds 91-92, 8h. Compared accepted orders, fills, net position and price drift for the round_trip role.
finding: The under-funded desk did 32 fills in an 8h run. Its 5111 accepted sells almost never filled, so it was not the persistent seller the accepted-order counts suggested; it was effectively absent from the market. Price drift shows no consistent direction across the fix (-2.14 to -1.77 on one seed, -1.59 to -2.57 on the other), which is what absence rather than distortion predicts. After funding, the desk does about 1000 fills and is symmetric, with net position under 1 ABC on both seeds.
correction: Corrects the claim made when the defect was found, that the desk was a one-sided seller biasing the price path and leaving makers systematically long. Accepted-order counts were read as flow; only fills are flow.
implication: Every FFA run to date lacked the inventory mean-reversion mechanism the round-trip desk was added to provide, and carried 79k wasted requests per run in the population's request stream. The missing mechanism matters most for maker inventory studies; the wasted requests matter for any rate-limit measurement taken over population totals.
open: Post-fix the desk places 13187 buy orders for 492 fills, a 3.7% conversion. That asymmetry between placed and filled is unexplained and may be a second defect in its quoting.
caveats: Two seeds.
Detected only because the metaorder defect prompted a reject-rate audit broken out by role, which had not been done in 190 experiments.

title: Fill loss is a clean sublinear function of admitted-throughput deficit
design: Swept metaorder_trader orders_per_day over 2000, 3000, 4500, 6000, 8000, 12000 on def_control.json, seed 91, 8h, holding the seed fixed so the dose varies by design rather than by draw. Dose = 1 - admitted_budgeted/admitted_control. Response = filled-quantity loss. Post the INVALID_QTY fix (4981384), pre the round-trip funding fix (f37b702).
finding: Across a 0 to 64% dose range the relationship is close to linear with slope 0.836 and R2 0.989, and the intercept is within a percentage point of zero. Denying the desk a tenth of its admitted requests costs it about 8.4% of executed quantity. Parent-count loss tracks quantity loss at every point, confirming the throughput mechanism from E-192 and E-194.
methodological_finding: This resolves what three rounds of per-seed ratios could not. Ratios taken at one cap ranged from 0.16 to 2.19 and were read as seed disagreement; they were an unstable estimator sampling one noisy point of this line. Sweeping the dose within a fixed seed turns the same underlying relationship into a tight fit. The intercept is the check the ratio form could never provide: a nonzero intercept would have meant the dose variable was contaminated.
caveats: One seed. E-197 replicates on seeds 91-92.
Ran on the population that lacked a working round-trip desk (f37b702), so the slope describes a market missing its inventory mean-reversion mechanism. E-197 re-runs against the corrected population.
Sublinearity is measured, not explained. The slope below one may be saturation at high dose rather than a uniform property; the two highest-dose points sit furthest below the line.
next: E-197: same sweep on the corrected population, seeds 91 and 92, with a 1500 cap added to extend the dose range.

title: Restoring the round-trip desk halves maker inventory
design: Compared maker_state inventory series across commit f37b702 on def_control.json, seeds 91-92, 8h, 5 spot makers per run. The desk's stated purpose is to return maker inventory through symmetric round trips, so the directional prediction was fixed by its design before measuring.
finding: Mean absolute maker inventory falls 53% on seed 91 and 21% on seed 92, standard deviation falls on both, and mean inventory moves toward zero on both. The desk delivers the inventory mean reversion it was added for, which the population has been missing.
correction: Without the desk, makers ran systematically short (-124 and -109), not long as guessed when the defect was found. The direction was observable in maker_state throughout and did not need to be guessed.
caveats: Two seeds, five makers, one configuration.
Adding roughly 1000 symmetric fills changes more than inventory; the inventory effect is the pre-specified prediction, but other differences between these runs are not controlled.
Effect size differs a lot between seeds (53% against 21%).
open: The desk converts only 3.7% of placed orders into fills because cross() sends IOC at the touch rather than through it, so the touch has moved by arrival. Metaorder children, which price through the touch with a slippage allowance, convert 27-43%. A stronger desk would likely show a larger effect.

title: Sub-minimum orders were pure waste: removing 44k requests per run leaves the market identical
design: A/B of commit 9331329 on def_control.json, seed 91, 8h. Compared accepted orders, fills and rejects per role.
finding: Rejects go to zero while accepted orders and fills are identical to the unit. The orders removed could never have traded, so the fix is pure waste removal with no behavioural change and determinism preserved.
implication: Population request totals in this campaign carried roughly 44k guaranteed-invalid requests per 8h run. Any rate-limit measurement taken over population totals rather than per-role admitted counts was inflated by that amount. Per-role measurements of metaorder_trader, which is what E-195 and E-197 use, are unaffected.
open: carry_arb still converts only 6.8% of accepted orders into fills, and round_trip 7.4%. Both send IOC at the touch rather than through it, so the touch has moved by arrival. This is a design property, not a rejection, but it means both desks are much weaker than their request counts suggest.

title: The dose response is concave, not linear: a binding budget costs about 25% of quantity almost immediately
design: Replication of E-195's cap sweep on the corrected population (post 4981384 and f37b702, pre 9331329), seeds 91-92, caps 1500-6000, 8h. Dose = per-role admitted-throughput deficit, response = filled-quantity loss.
finding: The linear model does not replicate. E-195's slope 0.836 with R2 0.989 and a near-zero intercept becomes 0.687 and 0.493 across two seeds, with a pooled intercept of +0.081 that survives seed averaging. The intercept is not noise: it is what fitting a line to a concave curve produces. Between zero and 15% deficit the loss reaches 25.3%, a local slope near 1.7; between 15% and 76% it only reaches 54.9%, a local slope near 0.48.
refines: E-195's claim of uniform sublinear harm with slope 0.836. That fit sampled no point between 0 and 6.8% deficit on one seed and mistook the average of a curve for a constant.
mechanism_hypothesis: A threshold rather than smooth concavity. Seed 92 at 8.5% deficit loses 23.9% and seed 91 at 21.6% loses 26.8%: a 2.5x difference in dose produces almost no difference in harm. This fits E-193's finding that binding budgets delay the start of the next parent rather than slowing the current one, which would cost a roughly fixed slice of throughput as soon as the budget binds at all.
caveats: Two seeds. The cap-2000 point has a 19.5 point spread between them, so individual points are not reliable even where the averaged curve is smooth.
No point sampled between 0 and 8.5% deficit, which is exactly where the threshold would sit. E-200 probes it.
Ran before the sub-minimum sizing fix (9331329), so the population still carried 44k invalid requests per run. Per-role metaorder counts are unaffected by that.
next: E-200 sweeps caps 6500-8000 on both seeds to locate the threshold, if it is one.
